notes.b: Some sporting events are built for the crowd taking part rather than for the winner. Knowing exactly what the term means is the starting point for the business and enterprise opportunities they create.
points: Mass-participation sporting events are organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, so beginners and experienced athletes share the same start line.
The usual aim is personal challenge, health or charity, rather than winning, which is why finishing is the goal for most entrants.

Types include city marathons (long-distance road races through a city), fun runs, parkrun (a free weekly timed run), cycling sportives (organised long-distance bike rides for all abilities), open-water swims, obstacle and colour runs, and triathlons (swim, cycle and run in one event).
notes.tip: If asked to define mass-participation sporting events, include large numbers, mixed ability, taking part at the same time, and the aim of challenge, health or charity rather than winning. Then give two examples.

notes.b: Ireland has well-known events that fit the definition. Naming real ones, with a fact about each, makes an answer specific.
points: Dublin Marathon: a marathon (a long-distance road race) held in Dublin each year.
Women's Mini Marathon: a women's mass-participation event in Dublin, so it is an example of a women-only format.
parkrun: a free, weekly, timed 5 km event held on Saturday mornings, so anyone can take part at no cost.
Great Limerick Run: a mass-participation running event in Limerick.
notes.tip: When asked to give examples of mass-participation events, name the event and where it is held, such as the Dublin Marathon in Dublin or the Great Limerick Run in Limerick.

notes.b: The number of people entering these events has grown because several things have made taking part more appealing and easier. Each reason below is one cause you can use to explain the growth.
points: Health and fitness awareness, promoted nationally, has encouraged more people to look for an activity to take up, and an organised event gives them one.
Charity fundraising and personal challenge goals attract entrants, such as 'bucket list' events (events people want to complete at least once in their lives).
Social media, apps and wearable trackers (watches and devices that record your runs) make training and sharing results easy, so participants stay motivated and show others what they achieved.
Inclusive formats widen who can enter: walk, jog or run options, shorter distances, women-only events and free weekly events.
Sponsorship (companies paying to be linked with the event) and professional event organisers, who market events widely, make events better known and better run.
Running and cycling clubs, couch-to-5k style programmes (plans that take a beginner from no running to a 5 km run) and workplace challenges give people a route into the events.
notes.tip: A question on how growth has provided opportunities for business needs causes and their business effect. Link each reason, such as sponsorship or apps and trackers, to the businesses that gain.

notes.b: A large crowd of participants and spectators is a market. For each opportunity, know what it is and who benefits.
points: Entry fees: each participant pays to enter, which is income for the organiser and for charities.
Title and partner sponsorship: a company's name is attached to the event (title sponsor) or it supports it as a partner, so brands gain exposure to thousands of participants and spectators.
Merchandise and event products: branded T-shirts, medals and photographs are sold, so the organiser and the event brand benefit from sales.
Retail: running shoes, clothing, watches, trackers and nutrition products are bought for training, so sports retailers benefit.
Services: coaching, training plans and apps, physiotherapy, sports massage and timing companies (who record each runner's time) are needed, so these providers benefit.
Local economy: hotels, restaurants, pubs, shops and transport are busy on event weekends with visitors from outside the area, so local businesses benefit.
Media and advertising: live and online coverage carries sponsors' brands to viewers beyond the start line, so broadcasters and advertisers benefit.

Charities raise large sums through participants' fundraising, because entrants ask friends, family and colleagues to sponsor them. Enterprise: new businesses are set up to organise events, sell event photography, provide timing chips (devices that record a runner's time) or run training groups, and their founders benefit.
notes.tip: To describe an opportunity, say what it is and who benefits, for example sponsorship gives brands exposure to thousands of participants and spectators. Choose opportunities from the event itself, such as entry fees, merchandise, retail, services or local spending.

notes.b: Events do more than make money. They also bring gains for the people taking part and the communities around them.
points: Health: participants gain fitness and wellbeing from the training and from taking part.
Goal-setting: a fixed event date gives participants a training target to work towards.
Community spirit: people train, cheer and volunteer together.
Inclusivity: events welcome people of mixed ability, so beginners are not shut out.
Charity income: money is raised for good causes through fundraising.

notes.b: Large events also have downsides. These are the costs and problems that organisers and communities have to deal with.
points: Road closures cause disruption to residents, because roads along the route are shut for the event.
Policing and stewarding costs (stewards guide participants and manage the route) must be met, which adds to the cost of running the event.
Litter and environmental impact, since thousands of people on a route leave waste behind.
Rising entry fees exclude lower-income groups, which works against the inclusive aim of these events.
Injury risk for participants who are unprepared, such as those who take on a distance without enough training.
Events can be dominated by commercial interests rather than by participants, so the business side outweighs the participants' needs.

keyTerms.definition: An organised event in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for personal challenge, health or charity rather than to win.
A mass-participation cycling event, usually on open roads, for riders of mixed ability.
A swimming event held in natural open water, such as a lake or the sea.
A mass-participation run with physical obstacles set along the route.
The organised supervision of an event by trained staff or volunteers to manage crowds and safety.
The amount each participant pays to take part in an event.
A device worn on the body that records activity, such as steps, heart rate and distance.
A structured training plan that takes a beginner from little or no running to running 5 km.
Raising money for a good cause, often through sponsored participation in an event.
An activity or event organised by an employer to encourage staff to take part in sport.
Branded products, such as T-shirts, medals and photographs, sold to participants and spectators.

questions.prompt: Examine the growth of mass-participation sporting events and the opportunities for business and enterprise they provide.
questions.model: Mass-participation events have grown because health and fitness awareness is promoted nationally, and because charity fundraising and personal challenge goals give people a reason to enter. Social media, apps and wearable trackers make training and sharing results easy, while inclusive formats such as walk, jog or run options, shorter distances and women-only events widen the range of people who take part. Running and cycling clubs, couch-to-5k programmes and workplace challenges bring newcomers in, and sponsorship and professional event organisers market events widely. This growth creates business opportunities. Entry fees bring income to the organiser and to charities, and title and partner sponsorship gives brands exposure to thousands of participants and spectators. Branded T-shirts, medals and photographs give income to the organiser and the event brand. Retailers sell running shoes, clothing, watches, trackers and nutrition products bought for training, and services such as coaching, training plans, physiotherapy, sports massage and timing companies serve participants. Local hotels, restaurants, pubs, shops and transport are busy on event weekends with visitors from outside the area. Media coverage carries sponsors' brands to viewers, and new enterprises can organise events, sell event photography, provide timing chips or run training groups. The Dublin Marathon, the Women's Mini Marathon, parkrun and the Great Limerick Run each illustrate these opportunities. The growth also brings costs, such as road closures and litter, and rising entry fees can exclude lower-income groups.

questions.prompt: Define mass-participation sporting events, give two examples and outline two opportunities they provide for businesses.
questions.model: Mass-participation sporting events are organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for personal challenge, health or charity rather than to win. Two examples are the Dublin Marathon and parkrun. Two opportunities for businesses are: first, merchandise, as branded T-shirts, medals and photographs are sold to participants, giving income to the organiser and the event brand; second, retail, as runners buy running shoes, clothing, watches and trackers for training, giving income to sports retailers.
